title: Take the Small Competitor With the Right Shape Seriously
documentTitle: Email from Neal Mohan to Scott Spencer et al. Re: OpenX Market Launches (April 21, 2009)
excerptForBlog:
OpenX is the only relatively smaller player to offer the same three-pillared approach to the display market as us, Yahoo, MSFT and AOL — platform, exchange and network. Therefore I think we need to take them even more seriously than the other exchanges / yield managers that are gaining traction out there (Rubicon etc.). For what its worth I think Tim (their CEO) is really good, understands exchanges and is on top of all the various data derivative options they can plug in or build. And they are focused on signing a big brand name publisher on their ad server to start gaining more credibility among the premium pubs.

Overall we are seeing OpenX, AdMeld, Rubicon and Pubmatic all moving towards the exchange model. This validates the market need but creates a more competitive environment. The key differentiators will be the liquidity available (buyers and sellers) as well as the robustness of the system for 3rd parties.

Additional competitive gaps noted in OpenX: No true dynamic allocation; no integration with buy-side platform; no Real-time Bidder; no Ad Quality controls; no Inventory Quality controls. On supply, Google had 370B impressions per month versus OpenX's 18B, and 1M buyers in AdWords plus 150 networks in AdX versus OpenX's very few.

lessonTitle: Take the Small Competitor With the Right Shape Seriously
pullQuote: Scale wins fights, but a competitor copying your structure can become a real threat long before they look like one on paper.
leadershipTraits: ranks competitors by structure, not size
situation: In April 2009, Google executive Neal Mohan emailed colleagues Scott Spencer and Joerg Heilig about a rising competitor, OpenX. The email is an internal competitive assessment. At stake: whether Google's display ad business would stay dominant as smaller players built the same multi-part stack Google had — ad server, exchange, and network — all in one.
insight: Mohan flags OpenX as uniquely dangerous because it mirrors Google's own structure: 'the same three-pillared approach.' That framing is the key move. He isn't worried about a niche threat; he's worried about a structural copycat with a capable CEO who 'understands exchanges.' The fact that OpenX, AdMeld, Rubicon, and Pubmatic are all converging on the exchange model is treated as a signal, not noise — 'this validates the market need but creates a more competitive environment.' That's classic competitive moat thinking: your lead is only as durable as the gaps you protect. Mohan then lists those gaps precisely — no real-time bidding, no buy-side integration, no ad quality controls — and anchors them in raw scale numbers: 370 billion impressions per month versus OpenX's 18 billion. The lesson isn't that Google is safe. It's that Mohan knows exactly where the moat is and wants his team to see it the same way.
application: Once a month, list the five concrete capabilities separating you from your closest competitor — not vague advantages, but specific missing features or data gaps on their side. When you see rivals converging on your model, update that list immediately. The convergence is your warning shot.
